This document outlines the methodology employed to construct the **GavelBench Leaderboard**, designed with aim evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) across multiple dimensions of relevance to deployment in Nav and public administration more widely.

The primary objective of this framework is to move beyond simple aggregate scores and standardised benchmarks that may fail to capture the nuanced legal, procedural and structural requirements of public administration or that mask critical failure modes (such as hallucination or factual deviation), and provide a principled methodology for a first order assessment of LLM utility in the context of public administration. Beyond measures of utility, Gavelbench aims to integrate dimensions of trustworthy AI, including safety, bias, transparency, and sustainability, into a comprehensive score with aim to provide a holistic view of LLM utility, performance and risk in the context of public administration.

:::{.callout-warning title="Disclaimer"}
GavelBench is under development and the methodology and evaluation framework still is still very much a *"work-in-progress"*. It is not intended to be a definitive or final evaluation of any model, and the results should not be interpreted as such. Moreover, the methodology is **not intended to be prescriptive or exhaustive**, as it most certainly **does not adequately capture all relevant dimensions of model performance or risk**. Evaluation methodology and scoring criteria will evolve over time as new insights and best practices emerge in the field of AI evaluation. The framework is designed to be transparent, reproducible, and adaptable, allowing for continuous improvement and refinement as new insights and best practices emerge in the field of AI evaluation.

Users are encouraged to interpret the results in the context of their own use cases and requirements, and to supplement the evaluation with additional testing and validation as appropriate. With time, we hope GavelBench will be extended with more processs-based and context-specific measures.
:::


## Methodology Overview

The GavelBench evaluation methodology provides the following three-prong assessment of how well the LLM:

- A) ...is able to answer questions specifically related to Nav's various benefits and services.
- B) ...performs on a range of tasks typically encountered in public administration, including summarization, instruction following, and question answering.
- C) ...aligns with Nav's principles of responsible AI deployment, including safety, bias, transparency, and sustainability.

These are detailed further below.

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" title="Domain-specific evaluation"}
### Domain-specific evaluation

In order to evaluate how well the LLM performs on questions specifically related to Nav's various benefits and services, we assess the model response to a set of questions that cover a range of topics relevant to public administration. The questions are drawn from a dataset of real-world questions submitted to Nav Kontaktsenter (NKS), and the model responses are evaluated against a set of reference answers generated by the RAG-system Bob and quality-checked by domain experts. As such the questions are representative of the types of questions that Nav receives from the public, and hence could reasonably be expected to query a commercially available LLM-based system. The questions vary in degree of complexity and specificity, and cover a wide range of topics relevant to Nav, including but not limited to: eligibility criteria for benefits, procedural requirements, and legal obligations.

The asssessment aims to test the model's ability to understand and generate accurate, relevant and contextually appropriate responses to questions that are representative of the types of questions that Nav receives from the public. To this end it employs a mixture of statistical, embedding-based, and LLM-judge based metrics to evaluate the model's performance against the reference answers. The metrics are listed in table @tbl-metrics.


::: {#tbl-metrics collapse="true"}
| Metric Type | Metric Name | Description | Interpretation (High vs Low Values) |
|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------------------------------|
| Statistical Metrics | ROUGE-L | Measures n-gram overlap between the model and reference answers. | **High** = Better lexical overlap with reference (stronger surface-level matching). <br> **Low** = Less word-for-word correspondence (possible paraphrasing or divergence). |
|                  | BERTScore | Evaluates semantic similarity using contextual embeddings. | **High** = Greater semantic alignment with reference despite vocabulary differences. <br> **Low** = Weaker meaning preservation; may convey different ideas. |
| Embedding-based Metrics | Cosine Similarity | Assesses vector similarity in embedding space. | **High** (~1.0) = Nearly identical semantic vectors; responses are closely aligned. <br> **Low** (~0 or negative) = Vectors point in different directions; semantically distinct content. |
|                  | Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) | Quantifies distributional divergence between model and reference outputs. | **High** = Greater distributional difference (outputs follow different patterns). <br> **Low** (~0) = Outputs follow nearly identical probability distributions. |
| LLM-judge based Metrics | NLI Entailment | Assesses whether the model's response entails the reference answer. | **High/Yes** = Model's response logically supports/implies the reference. <br> **Low/No** = Response contradicts or is unrelated to the reference (neutral/contradiction). |
|                  | Factual Correctness (FC) | A binary metric indicating whether the model's answer is factually accurate relative to the reference. | **High (1)** = Factually accurate according to reference. <br> **Low (0)** = Contains hallucinations or factual errors. |
: List of statistical, embedding-based and LLM-as-a-judge based metrics employed to assess responses to Nav-related queries
:::

* *Summarization*: Evaluates the model's ability to condense information while preserving key points and context.
* *Instruction Following*: Assesses how well the model adheres to specific instructions or prompts, including multi-step reasoning tasks.
* *Translation*: Measures the model's capability to accurately translate text between languages, maintaining meaning and nuance.

:::{.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" title="Responsible AI evaluation"}
### Alignment with responsible AI principles
some text...
:::

The final **composite score** is computed using a *Weighted Geometric Mean* of the normalized metric scores, with hard safety gates applied to critical metrics (specifically Factual Correctness) to ensure that models failing these gates are disqualified from ranking. The composite score is computed in a set of predefined categories:

```{python collapse="true"}
import json

def extract_overkategorier(file_path):
    with open(file_path, 'r') as file:
        data = json.load(file)

    overkategorier = [item['overkategori'] for item in data if 'overkategori' in item]
    overkategorier = [item for sublist in overkategorier for item in sublist]

    overkategorier = list(set(overkategorier))  # Remove duplicates

    # Generate markdown list
    markdown_list = "\n".join(f"* {kategori}" for kategori in overkategorier)
    return markdown_list

# Usage
file_path = './data/kategorier_mapping.json'
overkategorier_list = extract_overkategorier(file_path)
print(overkategorier_list)
```

allowing for category-specific evaluation and ranking. The area-specific scores are then aggregated into a final leaderboard ranking. The final leaderboard ranking also draws on draws on other benchmarks to capture a holistic view of model performance across multiple dimensions pertaining to:

    * Sustainability and environmental impact
    * Safety and harmful content
    * Openness and transparency
    * Bias and stereotyping
    * Privacy and legal compliance

These are included to reflect Navs principles of [responsible AI deployment](https://aksel.nav.no/god-praksis/artikler/prinsipper-for-ansvarlig-ki-i-nav).


## Leaderboard construction

Traditional leaderboard approaches often rely on arithmetic means of diverse metrics. This creates a "masking effect" where a model with high fluency but poor factual accuracy can achieve a deceptively high overall score.

To counteract this, the Gavelbench methodology adopts two critical principles:

1.  **Geometric Aggregation:** We utilize the Weighted Geometric Mean rather than the Arithmetic Mean. This mathematical approach ensures that a low score in *any* dimension disproportionately lowers the final composite score, enforcing a high baseline performance across all categories.
2.  **Hard Safety Gates:** Critical metrics may act as binary pass/fail gates. A model failing these gates immediately receives a "disqualifying score", regardless of performance in other areas. (It is worth noting that the safety gates are meant to be indicative and not definitive. Failing the safety gates does not necessarily imply that a model is unsafe for deployment, but rather that it has failed to meet the minimum threshold for a key benchmark metric in this evaluation context.)

### Geometric Mean Calculation for LLM Leaderboards

To calculate the **Weighted Geometric Mean** ($G$) for a set of $n$ normalized metrics ($m_i$) with corresponding weights ($w_i$), we use the following formula:

$$ G = \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n} m_i^{w_i} \right)^{\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j}} $$

where

- $m_i$: The normalized score (range $[0, 1]$) for metric $i$.
- $w_i$: The weight assigned to metric $i$.
- $\sum w_j$: The sum of all weights (the normalization factor).

:::{.callout-tip title="Why do we use the gemetric mean instead of the arithmetic mean?"}
Unlike the arithmetic mean, the geometric mean is highly sensitive to low values. If any single metric $m_k$ approaches zero, the entire product approaches zero, causing the final composite score to plummet. This mathematically enforces the **"no weak links"** policy essential for safety-critical AI evaluation, ensuring that high performance in fluency cannot mask a failure in factual correctness.
:::

:::{.callout-note title="A note on numerical stability" collapse=true}

Directly computing $\prod m_i^{w_i}$ can lead to **numerical underflow** (resulting in `0.0`) when dealing with small probabilities or many multiplied terms. To prevent this, the calculation is performed in **log-space**:

1.  Apply the natural logarithm ($\ln$) to transform the product into a sum:
    $$ \ln(G) = \frac{1}{\sum w} \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot \ln(m_i) $$

2.  Exponentiate the result to return to the original scale:
    $$ G = \exp\left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \ln(m_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j} \right) $$

**Edge Case Handling:** Since $\ln(0)$ is undefined ($-\infty$), a small epsilon value ($\epsilon = 10^{-9}$) is added to every metric before taking the logarithm to ensure numerical stability without significantly altering the score.
:::

## Input Format
The evaluation engine consumes data from a directory containing individual JSON files for each model candidate. Each file follows a standardized schema containing normalized metric scores:

```json
{
  "non_llm_string_similarity": 0.0635,
  "rouge_score(mode=fmeasure)": 0.2894,
  "semantic_similarity": 0.8913,
  "fc_high_high(mode=f1)": 0.105,
  "answer_correctness": 0.328
}
```

```{mermaid}
graph LR;
    RefA[Questions]-->B[LLM Respons];
    B-->C[statistical metrics];
    RefB[Answers]-->C;
    B-->D[judge metrics];
    RefB[Answers]-->D;
```
